query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting heavier refractory elements (e.g., tungsten) with aluminum in a near-equiatomic WMoNbTa-based refractory high-entropy alloy introduces stable B2 precipitates that enhance high-temperature mechanical properties while reducing density and preserving room-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast near-equiatomic WMoNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy before aluminum addition.
generation.intervention: Replace a fraction (e.g., up to about 5 at.%) of tungsten with aluminum via vacuum arc melting and subsequent forging.
generation.conditions: Homogenize at ~1200 °C, then perform tensile and creep testing from room temperature to ~1200 °C under inert atmosphere to evaluate mechanical performance and microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: B2 precipitates formed within the bcc matrix after partial aluminum substitution.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening conferred by B2 phases that hinder dislocation motion at high temperatures, combined with overall density reduction due to substituting a heavy element with a lighter one.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an unmodified WMoNbTa baseline, the Al-doped alloy will exhibit higher strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures (≥ 1100 °C), reduced density, and comparable room-temperature ductility and yield strength.
generation.baseline: Undoped WMoNbTa-based refractory high-entropy alloy manufactured under similar conditions and tested at identical temperatures and loading levels.
generation.boundary: Exceeding the solubility limit of Al or testing above the thermal stability range of the B2 phase can negate the strengthening benefits and lead to unwanted phases or embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al content and long-term stability of B2 precipitates under sustained high temperatures remain to be established experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloy variants: a baseline WMoNbTa alloy and an Al-doped variant (5 at.% Al substituted for W). Vacuum-arc melt, homogenize, and forge both alloys in the same conditions. Subject both to density measurement, tensile tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1200 °C, and creep tests at 1100–1200 °C. Examine the microstructure via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect B2 precipitates.
measurements: Density and chemistry to confirm target compositions and weight reduction
Tensile yield strength and ductility at room temperature and 1100–1200 °C
Creep life or rupture time at elevated temperatures
Microstructural characterization (B2 phase fraction and morphology) by SEM and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not show reduced density, enhanced high-temperature mechanical performance, or the expected B2 phases under the specified conditions, the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. chosen.lever: Partial Al replacement of heavier refractory elements
chosen.technique: Arc melting, vacuum arc remelting, forging, and heat treatment
chosen.conditions: Mechanical testing (tensile, creep) from RT to ~1200 °C; microstructure analysis via SEM/EBSD
chosen.why: Replacing heavier elements (like W, Mo) with Al in refractory HEAs can reduce density while forming B2-type precipitates that enhance high-temperature strength. This strategy preserves room-temperature performance by avoiding detrimental phases and employing established melting and forging processes common in HEA development.
